steps.body:
Two groups differ. Before you celebrate, ask the only question that matters:

**Could chance alone have produced a gap this big?**

To answer it, you need to know what gaps chance *does* produce. So build them: shuffle the labels at random, keeping the same scores, and record the gap. Do it hundreds of times.
Ten students, five per method. The new method averaged 15; the old one averaged 11.

widget.prompt: Relabel the same ten scores at random, again and again, to see what gaps chance manufactures. Then judge the real gap of 4.
widget.successFeedback: Chance hardly ever manufactures a gap of 4 from these ten scores — in the exact count, only 6 of the 252 possible splits reach it, about 2%. A gap that chance almost never produces is evidence of something other than chance.
widget.moreShufflesFeedback: Build the pile first. You cannot call a gap unusual until you have seen what usual looks like — keep relabelling.
widget.wrongVerdictFeedback: Look again at where the observed line falls: it sits out in the tail, with almost no random relabellings reaching it. That is the signature of a gap chance cannot easily fake.

cml.actionGoal: Shuffle labels under a null model and compare the observed statistic with the chance distribution.

explanationVariants: Shuffling the labels assumes the method made no difference — the same ten scores would have happened either way, and only the labels moved. That assumption is the null model.
The pile of shuffled gaps is a picture of 'what if there is no effect at all'. The real gap is then compared with it.

widget.prompt: When you shuffle the labels, what are you pretending is true?

options.label: The method has no effect on scores
options.feedback: Right. That pretence is the null model, and the pile of shuffled gaps shows exactly what it can produce.

options.label: The new method improves scores
options.feedback: The opposite. You assume it does NOT work, and then check whether the real data look like something that world could have produced.

options.label: The observed scores are random
options.feedback: The scores are held fixed — that is the point. Only the labels move, so any gap you see comes purely from which scores happened to land together.

options.label: The groups contain equal numbers
options.feedback: They are, but that is a detail of the setup rather than the assumption being tested.

explanationVariants: The pile of chance gaps is centred on 0, because with no real effect the two groups should differ only by luck, in either direction.
A pile centred anywhere else would mean the shuffling itself was tilted — which it is not.

widget.prompt: Your pile of shuffled gaps is centred on 0. Why?

options.label: Random labels favour neither group
options.feedback: Right. The null world has no reason to favour either label, so its gaps scatter symmetrically around 0.

options.label: The actual groups are identical
options.feedback: They are not — the real gap is 4. The pile is centred on 0 because it is built by pretending there is no effect, not because there is none.

options.label: All averages must equal zero
options.feedback: The averages here are 15 and 11, nowhere near 0. It is the DIFFERENCE under random relabelling that centres on 0.

options.label: The score values are too small
options.feedback: The size of the scores does not matter — shuffling their labels would centre the gap on 0 whatever the scale.

steps.body:
Now compare. The real gap was **4**. In the pile of chance gaps, almost nothing reaches out that far — in the exact count, 6 of the 252 possible splits, about **2%**.

So either something unusual happened by luck (about a 1-in-50 event), or the method really did something. That comparison is the whole logic of a significance test.

explanationVariants: Assume no effect → build what that world produces → see how rare your result is in it → decide whether 'luck' is still believable.
The test never proves the effect. It shows that the no-effect world struggles to produce data like yours.

widget.prompt: Put the four steps of a randomisation test in order.

items.label: Ask: how often does chance reach the real gap?
Record the gap from each relabelling
Shuffle the labels, keeping the scores

misorderFeedback.feedback: You cannot ask how rare the gap is until you have built the world it is supposed to be rare in. The assumption comes first.
There is nothing to record until you have shuffled. The shuffle produces the gap.

widget.missFeedback: Assume no effect, shuffle, record, then compare the real gap with the pile you built.
widget.successFeedback: Assume, shuffle, record, compare. The pile is not a decoration — it is the yardstick the real gap is measured against.

hints: The test tells you how well the NO-EFFECT world explains your data. Ask what follows from 'it explains it badly'.
About 2% of random relabellings reach a gap of 4. So under 'no effect', data like yours turn up about 1 time in 50.
That makes 'pure luck' an uncomfortable explanation. It does not make it impossible, and it does not measure how big the effect is.
explanationVariants: The careful conclusion: a gap this big is rare if the method has no effect (about 2%), so the data provide evidence against the no-effect model.
Note what is NOT concluded: nothing is proved, and nothing has been said yet about whether a 4-point gain is worth having.

widget.prompt: Only 2% of relabellings produce a gap of 4 or more. What may you conclude?

options.label: No effect is an implausible explanation
options.feedback: Right. The data count against the no-effect model; they do not prove the method works or establish the size of an effect.

options.label: There is a 2% chance of no effect
options.feedback: The 2% is the chance of seeing a gap this big IF the method does nothing — not the chance that the method does nothing. Those are different conditionals, and swapping them is the reversal error from the probability strand.

options.label: The method is proven effective
options.feedback: A 1-in-50 event does happen about 1 time in 50. Rare is not impossible, and a single study proves nothing.

options.label: The true effect is exactly 4 points
options.feedback: 4 points is this sample's estimate of the gain, and it wobbles like any estimate. The test asked whether there is an effect, not how big it is.

steps.body: Build the no-effect world, then check whether yours fits in it.
takeaways: Shuffle the labels while keeping the scores: that simulates a world where the treatment did nothing.
The pile of shuffled gaps centres on 0 and shows exactly what chance can manufacture.
If the real gap sits far out in that pile's tail, 'chance alone' becomes a poor explanation — which is not the same as proof.
steps.teaser: Next: how far out is far enough, and where the famous 5% comes from.

concept.body: The scores never change. Only the labels move. If the treatment truly did nothing, then the labels are just stickers — and any gap you see is an accident of which scores happened to get which sticker. Shuffling shows you every accident that was available.

explanationVariants: The scores stay exactly as measured; only the group labels are reassigned at random.
That is why the pile shows what chance alone could do with THESE scores.

widget.prompt: In a randomisation test, what gets shuffled?

options.label: The group labels — the scores stay put.
options.feedback: Right. Keeping the scores fixed is what makes the pile a fair picture of 'no effect'.

options.label: The scores — new random numbers each time.
options.feedback: Inventing new scores would test a different question. The whole point is to reuse the data you actually collected.
